title: City‐Wide Impacts of Cooling Infrastructure on Urban Outdoor Heat Stress of Populations With Diverse Physiological Characteristics
content:
Abstract

Adaptation strategies to reduce urban overheating are necessary to counteract rising trends in population exposure to extreme heat and associated health issues. The impact of these strategies has been traditionally assessed using only surface or air temperature (T a ), but some of these strategies may involve trade-offs and need to be evaluated using more comprehensive metrics. In this study, we combine a physiologically-based human heat balance model with a mesoscale meteorological model developed for outdoor thermal exposure to assess the impacts of street trees and cool (reflective) roofs, walls and pavement on heat stress across diverse populations. The study focuses on the hot and arid Las Vegas Valley and considers five representative personal profiles that combine different physical and behavioral characteristics. All strategies reduce daytime T a , but radiation effects dominate, leading to contrasting impacts on human heat stress across metrics. Street trees produce the smallest T a reductions but the largest heat stress benefit due to shade provision. In contrast, reflective walls and pavements increase heat stress by reflecting radiation toward pedestrians, even though they produce larger T a reductions. Under the assumption of continuous outdoor exposure, we find large differences across population groups, with the more sensitive profiles experiencing over twice as many hours of uncompensable heat stress relative to young individuals. Our results highlight the importance of considering context-specific profiles and examining the different avenues of heat exchange on humans when assessing the impacts of cooling strategies on urban overheating and heat stress.
